title: Our City, Our Schools
description: Before you teach in Washington, DC, learn the story of the place and the schools your students come from.
objectives: Describe the social, economic, and political context of Washington, DC.
Explain how segregation, desegregation, and disinvestment shaped DC schools, including the loss of Black educators.
Describe the dual landscape of DCPS and public charter schools, and the origins and mission of KIPP DC.
Say why knowing DC matters for your work with students and families.

blocks.text: You are about to teach children in a city with a long, specific, and often painful education history. Your students and their families know that history in their bodies, even if no one has ever taught it to them as a story. This section gives you the outline so that you can listen better once you meet them.

blocks.title: Your plan for the 68 minutes
blocks.text: Content (47 min), knowledge check (6), mindset check (5), final task (10). The audio episode is required and takes 31 minutes, so plan to listen in one sitting.

Washington is two cities that share a map. It is the seat of the federal government, a place of monuments and marble. It is also home to roughly 700,000 residents, a majority of whom are people of color, who live in neighborhoods with very different access to money, health care, grocery stores, and good schools.
Two facts frame everything else in this section.

**Wealth and poverty sit within a few miles of each other.** DC has some of the highest household incomes and some of the widest income gaps in the country. A family in a Northwest townhouse and a family in a Southeast apartment can live less than ten minutes apart and have almost nothing in common in resources. The Anacostia River has long been the dividing line in people's minds. Neighborhoods east of the river, in Wards 7 and 8, have received far less public and private investment.

**DC residents pay federal taxes but have no voting member of Congress.** The District has a mayor and a council, but Congress can overrule its laws and budget. You will see this show up in school funding, in policy debates, and on license plates that read "Taxation Without Representation."

**Participation looks different across communities.** Norms for eye contact, personal space, and turn-taking differ across cultures and families. A student who looks down while an adult speaks, or waits a few seconds before answering, may be showing respect or thinking carefully. You will meet students from many DC communities, so the habit to build is simple: notice, ask, and learn before you decide what a behavior means.

sections.title: Part 2. How DC's schools got here

blocks.text: Schools of excellence, built by Black Washington

Long before Brown v. Board of Education, Black Washingtonians built a school system under segregation and made it excellent. The best known example is the school that began in a church basement in 1870, five years after the Civil War. It became the M Street School and later Paul Laurence Dunbar High School, widely described as the first public high school for Black students in the United States. Its teachers held advanced degrees, many from top universities that would not hire them, and its graduates went on to Harvard, Oberlin, and Howard.

blocks.alt: Black-and-white photograph of students seated in rows in a classroom at the M Street High School in Washington, DC.
blocks.caption: Students and teachers at the M Street School, later Dunbar High School.
blocks.sourceNote: Search the Library of Congress Prints & Photographs collection (loc.gov/pictures) and the Washingtonian collection at DC Public Library. Confirm "no known restrictions" before use.

blocks.description: A one-minute introduction to Dunbar High School and where it started.

blocks.text: Desegregation and the loss of Black teachers

In 1954, Brown v. Board of Education ruled that segregated public schools are unconstitutional. It also set off one of the largest losses of Black professionals in American history. As Black schools closed or merged, thousands of Black teachers and principals were demoted, pushed out, or passed over for jobs. One researcher counts about 38,000 Black teachers displaced across the South alone in the decade after Brown. DC was not the same as the Deep South, but the national pattern left a long shadow on who stands at the front of classrooms.

This matters for your students today. Research reported by Chalkbeat finds that Black students who have even one Black teacher by third grade are more likely to graduate high school and enroll in college, and the effect grows with a second Black teacher. You may or may not be a Black teacher. Either way, you are entering a profession shaped by this history, and your students' families may remember it.
"Educationally and managerially bankrupt"

By the 1990s, DC Public Schools was in crisis. Reports described a system with crumbling buildings, patronage hiring, mismanaged money, and unreliable basic services. In 1996 a federal control board labeled it "educationally and managerially bankrupt." Decades of disinvestment, much of it in the neighborhoods that most needed support, had caught up with the children in them.
The reform era

Between 2007 and 2010, Mayor Adrian Fenty and Chancellor Michelle Rhee led an aggressive overhaul of DCPS: closing under-enrolled schools, changing teacher evaluation, and raising test-score expectations. Supporters point to real gains in test scores and enrollment. Critics point to school closures that hit Black neighborhoods hardest, teacher firings, and a testing scandal. Both things are part of the record, and you will meet educators and families who hold each view.

sections.title: Part 3. DC's education landscape and KIPP DC

blocks.text: In 1996, Congress and the District created the DC Public Charter School Board. Public charter schools are tuition-free public schools that are run independently of the traditional school district. Today almost half of DC's public school students attend charter schools, which makes DC one of the most charter-heavy cities in the country.

That "dual landscape" shapes what you will hear. Supporters credit charters with new options and strong results for many students. Critics point to closures, families being displaced from neighborhood schools, and a fragmented system in which families must navigate a lottery. It is also hard to compare DCPS and charters fairly, because they serve slightly different groups of students under different rules. Hold both perspectives. Your students' families have likely used both kinds of schools.
Where KIPP DC comes in

KIPP DC opened in 2001 with one school, KEY Academy, and 80 fifth graders. It began in a church basement in Anacostia, in Southeast DC. The founding belief was simple: a child's zip code should not decide their destiny. Over two decades the network has grown to serve more than 7,000 students from pre-K through 12th grade across campuses in Wards 2, 5, 7, and 8, and it started the Capital Teaching Residency so that new teachers could learn to teach here, with coaching, before leading a classroom alone.

Together with families and communities, we create joyful, academically excellent schools that prepare students with the skills and confidence to pursue the paths they choose—college, career, and beyond—so they can lead fulfilling lives and build a more just world.
Notice two phrases. *Together with families and communities* says the work is done with people, not to them. *The paths they choose* says the goal is student choice, not a single route.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the economic landscape of Washington, DC?

options.text: DC's poverty rate is lower than most major American cities
DC has high income inequality, with extreme wealth and concentrated poverty coexisting
DC is a uniformly wealthy city with few low-income residents

questions.explanation: DC has one of the highest income inequality rates of any major American city.

questions.prompt: What does research tell us about the impact of having a Black teacher on Black students?

options.text: There is no measurable difference in outcomes based on teacher race
Black students with at least one Black teacher are significantly more likely to graduate from high school and aspire to college
The impact only applies to students in elementary school

questions.explanation: Having even one Black teacher raises Black students' graduation rates and college aspirations.

questions.prompt: According to A Tale of Two Systems, what was the primary reason DCPS was labeled "educationally and managerially bankrupt" in the 1990s?

options.text: Significant underfunding relative to other major American cities
Decades of political corruption, patronage hiring, and systemic disinvestment in students
A lack of student motivation and family engagement in DC communities

questions.explanation: The reading points to political corruption, patronage hiring, and systemic disinvestment, not students or families.

questions.prompt: What does KIPP DC's mission mean when it says "the paths they choose"?

options.text: KIPP DC guides all students toward four-year college as the primary pathway
KIPP DC gives students skills and confidence to pursue their own paths: college, career, and beyond
KIPP DC allows students to opt out of academic expectations based on personal preference

questions.explanation: The mission is about students choosing their own paths, with the skills and confidence to pursue them.
